learn.hook: A sharp needle pierces your skin with a gentle push, while a wide-footed elephant walks on soft ground. Same physics: pressure.
points: Fluids (liquids and gases) flow; they cannot resist a shear stress and take the shape of their container.
Liquids are nearly incompressible (fixed volume); gases are highly compressible.
Pressure P = F/A (normal force per unit area). It is a scalar; SI unit pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²).
Small area → large pressure (sharp knife, needle). Large area → small pressure (wide foundations, snowshoes, broad straps of a school bag).
Density ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³); water ≈ 1000 kg m⁻³, mercury ≈ 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Relative density = ρ/ρ_water (dimensionless).

example.q: A 60 kg girl stands on one heel of area 1 cm². Find the pressure on the floor (g = 10 m s⁻²).

learn.reallife: Railway tracks rest on wide concrete sleepers so the enormous weight of a goods train is spread out and the ground doesn't sink.

topics.title: Pascal's law and pressure at depth

learn.hook: Divers in the Andaman Sea feel their ears pop just 3–4 m down. Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere of pressure.
points: Pascal's law: in a fluid at rest, pressure at a point is the same in all directions, and pressure is the same at all points at the same level (same depth).
Pressure at depth h below the open surface: P = P_a + ρgh, where P_a is atmospheric pressure.
The difference between two depths: P₂ − P₁ = ρg(h₂ − h₁).

Hydrostatic paradox: the pressure at the base depends only on the depth of liquid, not on the shape or volume of the vessel. Vessels of different shapes filled to the same height have equal pressure at the base.

example.q: Find the absolute pressure on a swimmer 10 m below the surface of a lake (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻², P_a = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa).

learn.reallife: Dams like Sardar Sarovar are built much thicker at the base because water pressure (and hence force per unit area) grows with depth.

learn.hook: The air above you presses on your palm with the weight of about 100 kg! You don't feel it because the pressure acts on all sides.
points: Atmospheric pressure at sea level: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa. It equals the pressure of a 76 cm (760 mm) column of mercury.
Torricelli's mercury barometer: a long tube of mercury inverted in a dish; mercury stands at h ≈ 76 cm, with near-vacuum above. P_a = ρgh. Units: 1 torr = 1 mm of Hg; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa.
Open-tube manometer: a U-tube with liquid; the difference in levels h gives the gauge pressure: P − P_a = ρgh.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with height (air becomes thinner), roughly halving every 5–6 km near the Earth.

learn.reallife: Mountaineers on the way to Ladakh's Khardung La notice breathlessness and chips packets puffing up: the outside air pressure is much lower up there.

topics.title: Hydraulic machines and forces on dams

learn.hook: A mechanic in a garage lifts an SUV with one hand on a lever. The secret is Pascal's law of transmission of pressure.
points: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the walls (Pascal's law of transmission).
Hydraulic lift: pressure F₁/A₁ on the small piston appears at the large piston, giving F₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁). Force is multiplied by the area ratio.
Work is not multiplied: the small piston moves farther (d₁A₁ = d₂A₂).
Hydraulic brakes in cars use the same principle: a small push on the brake pedal produces large forces on the brake shoes of all wheels.
Typical problems: pressure on a swimmer at depth; force on a dam; two-piston lifts.

example.q: In a hydraulic lift, the small piston has area 10 cm² and the large piston 1000 cm². What force on the small piston lifts a 1200 kg car? (g = 10 m s⁻²)

learn.reallife: Hydraulic jacks carried by truck drivers on national highways let one person lift a loaded wheel to change a tyre.

topics.title: Streamline flow and the equation of continuity

learn.hook: Press your thumb over a garden hose and the water shoots far. Narrow opening, faster flow: that's continuity.
points: Steady (streamline) flow: the velocity at each point does not change with time. Streamlines are the paths of fluid particles; they never cross.
A bundle of streamlines forms a flow tube. Above a critical speed, flow becomes turbulent (irregular, with eddies).
Equation of continuity (incompressible fluid, conservation of mass): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ (volume flow rate is constant).
Where streamlines crowd together (narrower region), the fluid moves faster.

example.q: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of area 10 cm² that narrows to 4 cm². Find the speed in the narrow part.

learn.reallife: Rivers like the Ganga flow slowly where they are wide (near Varanasi's ghats) and rush through narrow gorges in the Himalayas.

learn.hook: During a cyclone in Odisha, roofs are lifted off houses. Fast wind over the roof means low pressure above, while the air inside is still.
points: Bernoulli's principle: along a streamline, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant (for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow).
Derivation: apply the work–energy theorem to a fluid element in a tube of varying area and height. Work done by pressure forces = change in KE + change in gravitational PE.
Each term is energy per unit volume: pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy.
For a fluid at rest (v = 0), it reduces to P₁ − P₂ = ρg(h₂ − h₁), the pressure–depth relation.
Limitations: ignores viscosity (energy loss), compressibility and unsteady/turbulent flow.

example.q: Water flows horizontally through a pipe; speed changes from 2 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹. Find the pressure difference (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³).
steps: Same height, so P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².
= 6000 Pa (pressure is lower where the water is faster).

learn.reallife: The venturi in older scooter carburettors uses Bernoulli's principle: fast air in the narrow throat lowers pressure and sucks in petrol.

topics.title: Torricelli's law, dynamic lift and Bernoulli in action

learn.hook: A spin bowler makes the ball drift in the air; a passenger jet lifts hundreds of people off the runway at Delhi. Both are Bernoulli at work.
points: Speed of efflux (Torricelli's law): water from a small hole at depth h below the open surface of a large tank leaves at v = √(2gh), like a body falling freely through h.
Magnus effect: a spinning ball drags air around it; air moves faster on one side, so pressure is lower there and the ball swerves (dynamic lift).
Aerofoil (wing): air flows faster over the curved upper surface than below, so pressure above is lower; lift = ΔP × area = ½ρ(v_top² − v_bottom²)A.
Everyday effects: blowing over a strip of paper lifts it; an atomiser/spray uses fast air to suck liquid up; roofs are blown off in storms.

example.q: Air flows over a wing at 50 m s⁻¹ and under it at 40 m s⁻¹ (ρ = 1.2 kg m⁻³). Find the lift on a wing of area 20 m².

learn.reallife: Swing and drift in cricket owe a lot to air flow around the ball; spin bowlers use the Magnus effect to make the ball dip or drift.

learn.hook: Pour honey and water side by side: water races, honey crawls. The difference is viscosity, the fluid's internal friction.
points: Viscosity is internal friction between layers of a fluid in relative motion; it opposes the relative motion of layers.
In laminar flow, layers slide over each other with a velocity gradient v/l. Coefficient of viscosity η = (F/A)/(v/l), i.e. shear stress/strain rate.
SI unit: Pa s (also N s m⁻²); CGS unit poise (1 poise = 0.1 Pa s). Honey and glycerine have large η; water and air small η.
Temperature: viscosity of liquids decreases as temperature rises; viscosity of gases increases with temperature.
Example: a plate dragged over a thin oil film: η = Fl/(Av).

example.q: A metal plate of area 0.1 m² is pulled at 0.5 m s⁻¹ over a 1 mm oil film with a force of 0.5 N. Find η.

learn.reallife: Engine oils sold at Indian petrol pumps are graded by viscosity (like 20W-40) so they flow in a cold Shimla winter and still protect in hot Chennai summers.

learn.hook: Raindrops fall from clouds kilometres high but hit you gently. Air drag makes them stop accelerating and reach a steady terminal speed.
points: Stokes' law: a small sphere of radius a moving slowly at speed v through a fluid of viscosity η feels a drag force F = 6πηav.
As a sphere falls, drag grows with speed until weight = buoyancy + drag. Then acceleration is zero: terminal velocity v_t.
Balancing: (4/3)πa³ρg = (4/3)πa³σg + 6πηav_t gives v_t = 2a²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), where ρ is the sphere's density and σ the fluid's.
v_t ∝ a²: bigger drops fall faster. If ρ < σ (air bubble in water), v_t is negative: the bubble rises.

example.q: A steel ball falls in oil and reaches terminal velocity 2 cm s⁻¹. What would be the terminal velocity of a ball of the same material with twice the radius?

learn.reallife: Doctors at AIIMS use the Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) test: red blood cells settle at a nearly constant speed governed by Stokes-type drag. Lab safety: if you time steel balls falling through glycerine or oil, wipe up spills at once (the floor gets slippery) and drop the balls gently so the glass jar doesn't crack.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why raindrops don't keep speeding up all the way down. Explain Stokes' law and terminal velocity.

learn.hook: Water striders skate on ponds in Kerala's backwaters, and a steel needle can float on water. The surface acts like a stretched skin.
points: A liquid surface behaves like a stretched membrane. A molecule inside is pulled equally from all sides, but a surface molecule is pulled inward, so surface molecules have extra energy.
Surface energy: extra energy of the surface. To increase the surface area, work must be done.
Surface tension S = force per unit length acting along the surface, = surface energy per unit area (unit N m⁻¹ or J m⁻²).
Film on a wire frame with a movable slider of length l: the film has two surfaces, so F = 2Sl. Work to increase area by ΔA (each side) = S × 2ΔA.
Water at room temperature: S ≈ 0.072 N m⁻¹. Surface tension decreases as temperature rises.

example.q: A soap film (S = 0.03 N m⁻¹) is held on a frame with a movable slider of length 10 cm. Find the force needed to hold the slider.
steps: The film has two surfaces: F = 2Sl.

learn.reallife: Hot water and detergents clean oily dishes better because both reduce surface tension, helping water spread and wet the grease.

learn.hook: Water spreads on clean glass but beads up on a lotus leaf. The angle of contact decides whether a liquid wets a surface.
points: Angle of contact θ: the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid.
θ < 90°: the liquid wets the surface and spreads (water on clean glass, θ ≈ 0°). θ > 90°: the liquid does not wet it and forms drops (mercury on glass, water on wax or lotus leaves).
Balance of interfacial tensions at the edge: S_sa = S_la cos θ + S_sl (solid–air, liquid–air, solid–liquid).
If S_sl < S_sa, cos θ > 0 and θ is acute; if S_sl > S_sa, θ is obtuse.
Soaps and detergents lower the contact angle, so water wets cloth and grease better; waterproofing agents raise it.

example.q: For a liquid on a solid, S_sa = 0.05 N m⁻¹, S_sl = 0.02 N m⁻¹ and S_la = 0.06 N m⁻¹. Find cos θ and decide if the liquid wets the solid.
steps: θ = 60° < 90°, so the liquid wets the solid.

learn.reallife: Waterproof jackets used by trekkers in Meghalaya, one of the rainiest places on Earth, have coatings that make water's contact angle obtuse so it rolls off.

teach.ask: Gappu notices rain spreads on the window glass but rolls off a lotus leaf. Explain angle of contact and wetting.
teach.praise: Acute angle: it wets and spreads. Obtuse: it beads up. Detergents shrink the angle to wet things better!
teach.nudge: What is the angle of contact? What happens when it is less than 90°? More than 90°?

learn.hook: Plants pull water up through tiny tubes, and a cloth wick soaks up oil in a diya. Capillary action at work.
points: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop (one surface): Pᵢ − Pₒ = 2S/r. An air bubble inside a liquid also has one surface: 2S/r.
Soap bubble in air has two surfaces: Pᵢ − Pₒ = 4S/r. Smaller bubbles have larger excess pressure.
Capillary rise: h = 2S cos θ/(ρgr). Concave meniscus (θ < 90°, water in glass) rises; convex meniscus (θ > 90°, mercury) is depressed.
h ∝ 1/r: narrower tubes, higher rise.
Small drops are spherical because surface tension minimises the area; surface energy problems use W = S ΔA.

example.q: Water (S = 0.07 N m⁻¹, θ ≈ 0°) is in a glass tube of radius 0.7 mm (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the capillary rise.

learn.reallife: The wick of a traditional diya or kerosene lantern draws oil upward by capillary action between its fibres.
